title: Thin end of the wedge
gist: Resolution Foundation analysis finds that despite the UK's 2024-25 employer National Insurance hike producing the largest single-year tax-wedge increase across the OECD, the UK's tax burden on average and middle earners remains low by both international and historical standards, and concludes that funding rising defense/fiscal pressures (targeting 3.5% of GDP, +£28bn/year by 2035) will require broad-based tax rises on middle earners rather than relying solely on smaller tax heads.

themes.theme: UK tax wedge rose sharply but from a very low base

insights.claim: The UK experienced the largest rise in the tax wedge across the OECD in 2025 — a 2.4 percentage point increase — driven by Rachel Reeves' Autumn Budget 2024 decision to raise the employer National Insurance Contributions rate and lower the secondary threshold, plus fiscal drag from frozen tax thresholds while earnings grew.
insights.speaker: Matthew Cavanagh
insights.so_what: Confirms the 2024 Autumn Budget NICs change was the largest tax-wedge shock in the entire OECD for 2025 — a key data point for modeling UK employer labor costs and hiring incentives going forward.
insights.locator: The tax wedge has increased in the past couple of years section

insights.claim: Despite this record increase, the UK's tax wedge for a single average earner was 32.4% in 2025 — 2.7 percentage points below the OECD average — and the UK now ranks the 9th lowest among 33 rich OECD countries; before the increase the UK had the lowest tax wedge for an average earner in the G7, and the rise now puts it just below Ireland and Japan, overtaking the US and Canada.
insights.speaker: Matthew Cavanagh
insights.so_what: Precisely quantifies the UK's relative tax-competitiveness position for labor even after the largest OECD tax-wedge rise — supports the case that further UK tax increases on labor have room to run internationally before the UK becomes an outlier.
insights.locator: The tax wedge has increased in the past couple of years section

themes.theme: No country has both a bigger state and lower taxes on average workers

insights.claim: Using OBR's March 2026 estimate of UK tax revenues at 36.3% of GDP for 2025-26 (up from 34.4% in 2024, driven mainly by personal tax increases), the Foundation finds that of the 16 rich OECD countries raising more tax revenue as a share of GDP than the UK, every single one also imposes a higher compulsory payment wedge on a single average earner — with the sole partial exception of families with one earner and two children.
insights.speaker: Matthew Cavanagh
insights.so_what: Establishes a strong empirical constraint/mental model: no OECD country funds a bigger state without taxing average workers more, directly undercutting any UK political platform promising expanded public spending while sparing middle-earner taxation.
insights.locator: No country raises more in tax without also having a higher compulsory payment wedge section

insights.claim: The Foundation's core policy conclusion is that funding rising UK defense spending (a target of 3.5% of GDP, costing an additional £28 billion annually in today's terms by 2035 versus current plans) should come from broad-based tax rises that include typical/average earners, since 'any politician promising a bigger state and lower taxes on middle earners is not being realistic.'
insights.speaker: Matthew Cavanagh
insights.so_what: A direct, quantified policy prediction/prescription (£28bn/year additional defense cost by 2035) that flags likely future UK tax rises on middle earners as the fiscally 'realistic' funding path — relevant for forecasting UK personal tax policy and consumer disposable income trends into the 2030s.
insights.quote: This analysis strongly suggests that any politician promising a bigger state and lower taxes on middle earners is not being realistic.

themes.theme: Historical context: taxes on middle earners remain low

insights.claim: The overall effective tax rate for the median UK employee in 2025 remained lower than before the 2008 financial crisis, despite recent rises including the employer NICs increase; the sharpest recent increases have been for lower-paid employees (those at half the median wage), while higher earners (2x or 10x median) face rates somewhat above 2000s/2010s levels but still below historical peaks.
insights.speaker: Matthew Cavanagh
insights.so_what: Undercuts narratives that the UK tax burden on ordinary workers is at a historic high — median-earner effective tax rates remain below pre-2008 levels, giving fiscal policymakers more room than headline 'record tax burden' narratives suggest, though lower earners have seen the sharpest relative increases.
insights.locator: Taxes on middle earners remain low by historical standards section

themes.theme: Family/child benefit treatment and self-employment tax gap

insights.claim: The UK provides very limited generosity in cash benefits or preferential tax treatment for families with children compared to international peers: a one-earner married couple with two children in the UK has a compulsory payment wedge of 28.8%, only slightly below the 32.4% for a single individual, whereas other OECD countries treat such families much more favorably (the UK's compulsory-payment-wedge ranking improves only from 29th to 21st when moving from a single earner to a couple with children).
insights.speaker: Matthew Cavanagh
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, internationally-benchmarked policy gap (weak UK family tax relief) that could inform future UK budget proposals targeting family/child benefits as a politically popular reform lever distinct from headline income-tax changes.
insights.locator: The compulsory payment wedge...does not just consider taxes paragraph

insights.claim: Income from employment is taxed much more heavily than income from other sources in the UK, with the gap between tax on self-employment and tax on employment reaching record highs, meaning the report argues taxes on working (employed) families are not the obvious place for government to look first when balancing the books.
insights.speaker: Matthew Cavanagh
insights.so_what: Flags a record and growing tax-arbitrage gap between employment and self-employment in the UK — relevant to forecasting future UK tax reform targeting self-employed/incorporation structures (a recurring UK Budget theme) and to labor-structuring decisions by high earners.
insights.locator: Continuing to avoid raising taxes on middle earners section
